title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
formal: Determine the optimal polynomial separation exponent \[\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}=\inf\bigl\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ R(f)\le C\,Q(f)^a\bigr\}.\] Here \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) are randomized and quantum bit-query complexities with worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The constant \(C\) must be independent of both \(n\) and \(f\). The known range is \(3\le\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\le4\). This card makes the source's maximum-gap question precise at the level of its polynomial exponent; logarithmic factors are not part of this numerical target.
why: This quantifies the greatest possible quantum query advantage when an algorithm must handle every input, without a promise. It tests a basic limitation on quantum speedups and distinguishes the role of classical randomization from that of deterministic computation.
status_note: Open in Aaronson’s 2021 survey. The near-cubic lower-bound family and universal quartic bound were checked in their primary papers on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-work search found no resolution of the displayed exponent; the September 2026 paper Quantum Query Advantage Requires Space concerns an additional workspace restriction and does not close this gap.

progress.text: Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal establish the universal quartic deterministic-versus-quantum query bound, giving the upper endpoint four.
Bansal and Sinha obtain total Boolean functions with a near-cubic randomized-versus-quantum separation, giving the lower endpoint three.
Aaronson explicitly asks to close the gap between the cubic separation and quartic universal upper bound.

importance.reason: Determines the strongest quantum query advantage when the function has no promise, a basic limit on quantum computation.

sentences: The question asks for the largest polynomial quantum query advantage over randomized algorithms on total Boolean functions.
Both models must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input.
Only queries to input bits are counted, with other computation and workspace unrestricted.
Known results put the optimal separation exponent between three and four.
The target is to certify that exponent within one hundredth, without resolving finer logarithmic factors.

definitions:
A total Boolean function assigns one output bit to every length-\(n\) bit string, with no promise restricting the inputs. Nonconstant means that both output values occur. A deterministic decision tree adaptively chooses an input coordinate, receives its bit, and ultimately outputs a bit. Its depth is the maximum number of queries on a root-to-leaf path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic trees of depth at most \(T\). It must output \(f(x)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input \(x\). The least possible \(T\) is \(R(f)\); unlimited computation and storage between queries are free.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

Both complexities are positive integers for nonconstant functions and at most \(n\). The infimum takes all real nonnegative exponents with a universal multiplicative bound. An exponent at the infimum need not itself admit such a bound: logarithmic factors may prevent attainment. Removing constant functions avoids zero-complexity conventions. The approximation tolerance for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\) concerns the exponent itself, not a relative approximation to a query count.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a_*\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a_*-\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) suffices via its midpoint. It must control the universal upper bound and the existence of sufficiently large separations to certify this accuracy; merely improving one currently known bound does not suffice. The benchmark does not require resolving logarithmic factors or proving that the infimum exponent is attained.

context_blocks.text: Quantum algorithms can exploit a special promise to obtain enormous advantages over randomized algorithms. Total functions remove that freedom. Every input string must have a specified correct answer, so both the quantum algorithm and its classical competitors must handle adversarial inputs.

The quartic upper bound follows from \(R(f)\le D(f)=O(Q(f)^4)\), where \(D(f)\) is deterministic decision-tree depth. A matching separation between deterministic and quantum queries does not automatically give a matching separation against randomized algorithms.

The near-cubic lower-bound family comes from stronger promise-problem separations combined with a construction turning them into total functions. This establishes an exponent of at least three; it does not supply a quartic randomized separation.

The exponent formulation intentionally ignores subpolynomial factors. For example, an additional logarithmic factor in a universal cubic bound would still be compatible with exponent three. Establishing the exact bound with exponent three and no extra factor is a finer question.
